questions.prompt: Predict the output: a struct read out of a List and then modified.
questions.explanation: The List indexer returns a copy of the struct, so `p` is an independent value. Changing `p.X` to 5 does not touch the element stored in the list, which still has X = 1.

questions.prompt: Predict the output: assigning a class instance versus a struct instance and then mutating the copy.
questions.explanation: `b = a` copies a reference, so `a` and `b` point to the same object and `a.V` becomes 2. `t = s` copies the whole struct, so changing `t.V` leaves `s.V` at 1. The line is `2 1`.

questions.prompt: Predict the output: a positional record, `with` and record equality.
questions.explanation: `with` creates a new record and leaves `p1` unchanged, so p1 prints through the compiler-generated ToString as `Person { Name = Ann, Age = 30 }`. `p2.Age` is 31. Making another copy with Age = 30 gives a record whose properties all equal p1's, and record == compares values, so it prints True.

questions.prompt: Predict the output: calling string methods without using their return values.
questions.explanation: Strings are immutable: ToUpper and Replace return new strings that are thrown away, so `s` is still `hello`. `s += "!"` creates a new string and points `s` at it; `t` still refers to the old `hello`. Output: hello, hello, hello!.

questions.prompt: Predict the output: boxing an int and comparing boxed values.
questions.explanation: Boxing copies the value into a new heap object, so `o` keeps 1 after `x` changes. `a` and `b` are two separate boxes; `==` on `object` compares references, giving False. `Equals` is virtual and Int32.Equals compares the values, giving True.

questions.prompt: Predict the output: comparing strings through `string` and through `object` variables.
questions.explanation: With static type string, `==` calls the string overload and compares characters: True. With static type object, `==` is reference equality, and `b` is a separately allocated string: False. `Equals` is virtual, so String.Equals runs and compares contents: True. Literals are interned, so `a` and the literal "hi" are the same object: True.

questions.prompt: Predict the output: records whose property is an array.
questions.explanation: Record equality compares each property with EqualityComparer<T>.Default. For an array that is reference equality, so two different arrays with the same contents make the records unequal (False). When both records hold the very same array, the property compares equal and the records are equal (True).

questions.prompt: Predict the output: list patterns with a slice.
questions.explanation: `[]` matches only an empty array and `[var x]` exactly one element. `[1, .. var rest]` matches arrays starting with 1 and captures the remaining elements as a new array (length 3). `[9, 8]` does not start with 1, so the last arm binds first = 9 and last = 8.

questions.prompt: Predict the output: property patterns, type patterns and null in one switch.
questions.expectedOutput:
EU 5
big US
other order
int 42
null
unknown
questions.explanation: Each item takes the first matching arm. Order(5, EU) fails the first property pattern but matches Region EU. Order(150, US) matches `Total > 100` and Region US. Order(20, US) only matches the plain type pattern. 42 is an int, null hits the null pattern, and the string falls to the discard.

questions.prompt: Predict the output: lifted operators on a null `int?`.
questions.explanation: `??` substitutes -1 for null. Arithmetic on a null nullable yields null, so `a + 5 == null` is True. Lifted comparison operators (<, >, <=, >=) return false whenever an operand is null, so both `a > 0` and `a <= 0` are False. Lifted == treats two nulls as equal, so the last line is True.

questions.prompt: Predict the output: boxing a nullable value type.
questions.explanation: Boxing a Nullable<T> without a value produces a null reference, not a box holding an empty Nullable: True. Boxing a Nullable<T> that has a value boxes the underlying int, so GetType reports Int32 (there is no boxed Nullable<int>), and `o2 is int` is True.

questions.prompt: Predict the output: int overflow in the default unchecked context versus inside `checked`.
questions.explanation: Non-constant integer arithmetic is unchecked by default, so int.MaxValue + 1 silently wraps to int.MinValue, -2147483648. Inside `checked(...)` the same addition throws OverflowException, so `overflow` is printed instead.

questions.prompt: Predict the output: integer division and remainder with negative numbers.
questions.explanation: Integer division truncates toward zero: 7/2 = 3 and -7/2 = -3 (not -4). The remainder takes the sign of the dividend, so -7 % 3 = -1. With a double operand the division is floating point: 3.5.

questions.prompt: Predict the output: Math.Round on midpoint values and casting a double to int.
questions.explanation: Math.Round defaults to MidpointRounding.ToEven (banker's rounding): 2.5 goes to 2, 3.5 to 4, -2.5 to -2. AwayFromZero rounds 2.5 to 3. Casting a double to int truncates toward zero, so 2.7 becomes 2 and -2.7 becomes -2.

questions.prompt: Predict the output: comparing floating-point and decimal sums.
questions.explanation: 0.1 and 0.2 have no exact binary representation, so their double sum is slightly off 0.3: False. decimal is base 10 and represents them exactly: True. Floating-point division by zero yields infinity instead of throwing: True. A float has a 24-bit significand, so 16777217 (2^24 + 1) rounds to 16777216: True.

questions.prompt: Predict the output: NaN with ==, Equals, HashSet and Contains.
questions.explanation: IEEE 754 says NaN is not equal to anything, so `==` is False. Double.Equals is defined so that NaN equals NaN (to keep collections working): True. HashSet and Contains use EqualityComparer<double>.Default, which calls Equals, so the set holds one element and Contains finds it.

questions.prompt: Predict the output: deferred execution of a Where query versus ToList.
questions.explanation: A LINQ query is only a description until it is enumerated. Count() runs it after 4 was added, so it sees 2, 3 and 4: 3. ToList() runs the query immediately and stores the results, so adding 5 later does not change the snapshot: 3.

questions.prompt: Predict the output: the order in which Where and Select lambdas run while iterating.
questions.explanation: LINQ operators stream: each element flows through the whole pipeline before the next is pulled. 1 passes Where and Select and is printed; 2 is rejected by Where so Select never sees it; 3 passes both. The operators do not run one after another over the full list.

questions.prompt: Predict the output: GroupBy over a list of words.
questions.expectedOutput:
a: apple,avocado,ant
b: bob,banana
c: cat,cherry
questions.explanation: GroupBy yields groups in the order their keys first appear in the source (a, b, c), and the elements within each group keep their original relative order. It does not sort.

questions.prompt: Predict the output: OrderBy with equal keys, and a descending ThenBy.
questions.expectedOutput:
Bob Dee Ann Cid
Cid Ann Dee Bob
questions.explanation: LINQ's OrderBy is a stable sort, so people with equal ages keep their source order: Bob before Dee, Ann before Cid. In the second query ages are descending (30s first) and ties are broken by name descending: Cid, Ann, then Dee, Bob.

questions.prompt: Predict the output: Distinct on class instances, DistinctBy, and a custom comparer.
questions.explanation: Item does not override Equals/GetHashCode, so Distinct uses reference equality and all three instances are distinct: 3. DistinctBy compares the projected Id values (1, 1, 2): 2. With OrdinalIgnoreCase, "a" and "A" are equal: 2.

questions.prompt: Predict the output: First, Single and FirstOrDefault when there are several matches or none.
questions.explanation: First returns the first match, 3. Single requires exactly one match; 3 and 4 both match, so it throws InvalidOperationException. FirstOrDefault returns default(int) = 0 when nothing matches. Single(n > 3) has exactly one match, 4.

questions.prompt: Predict the output: lambdas capturing a `for` loop variable versus a `foreach` loop variable.
questions.explanation: A `for` loop declares one variable shared by all iterations; the lambdas capture that variable, which is 3 when they run, so they print 333. Since C# 5 each `foreach` iteration gets a fresh variable, so those lambdas print 0, 1 and 2.

questions.prompt: Predict the output: a lambda capturing a local that changes afterwards, and a counter closure.
questions.explanation: Lambdas capture variables, not values, so `f` reads x when called: 5 * 10 = 50. MakeCounter's local `c` lives on in the closure after the method returns; each call increments the same variable, so the third call returns 3.

questions.prompt: Predict the output: when the body of an iterator method actually runs.
questions.explanation: Calling an iterator method runs none of its body; it only creates the enumerator. `created` prints first. Enumerating runs the body up to the first yield (start, then 1). Take(1) stops asking after one element, so `middle` and `end` never print.

questions.prompt: Predict the output: breaking out of a foreach over an iterator with try/finally.
questions.explanation: After printing 1 the loop breaks. foreach disposes the enumerator, and disposing an iterator suspended inside a try runs its finally block, so `cleanup` prints before `after`. The second yield is never reached.

questions.prompt: Predict the output: argument validation inside an iterator method.
questions.expectedOutput:
got sequence
thrown on enumeration: negative
questions.explanation: Because the method contains yield, even the guard clause is deferred: calling Repeat(-1) succeeds and returns an enumerator. The exception only happens on the first MoveNext, inside the foreach. That is why library code puts validation in a non-iterator wrapper method.

questions.prompt: Predict the output: a `return` inside try with a finally block.
questions.explanation: The try block prints `try` and evaluates the return value, but before control leaves the method the finally block runs and prints `finally`. Only then does the caller get 1 and print it.

questions.prompt: Predict the output: a finally block that changes the variable being returned.
questions.explanation: `return x` evaluates and stores the value 1 before finally runs, so reassigning x afterwards has no effect: 1. In H the stored return value is a reference to the list; finally mutates that same object, so the caller sees one element: 1.

questions.prompt: Predict the output: an exception filter that returns false.
questions.explanation: The filter expression runs when the exception is being matched, so Log prints its message. It returns false, so the inner catch is skipped as if it did not match, and the exception continues to the outer handler, which prints `outer boom`. `inner` never prints.

questions.prompt: Predict the output: catch clause order and finally.
questions.explanation: ArgumentNullException derives from ArgumentException, so the first catch clause that fits is the ArgumentException one: B. Only one catch runs, so C is skipped. finally always runs: D.

questions.prompt: Predict the output: a finally block that throws while another exception is in flight.
questions.explanation: The first exception triggers the finally block. When finally throws, the new exception replaces the one in flight; the original is lost entirely, not attached as InnerException. The catch sees `second` and InnerException is null: True.

questions.prompt: Predict the output: code before and after the first await in an async method that is not awaited immediately.
questions.explanation: An async method runs synchronously on the caller's thread until its first await of an incomplete task. So Work prints 2 before returning a Task. The caller prints 3, then awaits; when the delay finishes, Work prints 4 and completes, and the caller prints 5.

questions.prompt: Predict the output: an async method that throws before any await.
questions.explanation: In an async method, exceptions are never thrown to the caller directly; they are captured into the returned Task. So calling Fail() returns a faulted task and `called` prints. The exception is rethrown when the task is awaited and caught there.

questions.prompt: Predict the output: the result order of Task.WhenAll with tasks that finish at different times.
questions.explanation: Task.WhenAll returns results in the same order as the tasks were passed in, regardless of which finished first. The squares of 3, 1 and 2 are 9, 1 and 4.

questions.prompt: Predict the output: writing through a Span slice versus a range-indexed array copy.
questions.explanation: A Span is a view over existing memory, so s[0] is arr[1] and writing 20 changes the array. The slice covers 3 elements. Applying a range to an array (arr[1..3]) allocates a new array copy, so writing 99 into it does not affect arr, which still has 20.

questions.prompt: Predict the output: Dictionary indexer assignment, Add with a duplicate key, and TryGetValue.
questions.explanation: The indexer setter adds or overwrites, so the value becomes 2. Add refuses an existing key and throws ArgumentException. TryGetValue on a missing key returns false and sets the out parameter to default(int), 0.

questions.prompt: Predict the output: Stack and Queue built from the same array.
questions.explanation: The Stack constructor pushes 1, 2, 3 in order, so 3 is on top and Pop returns it; the Queue dequeues from the front, 1. Enumerating a stack goes from top to bottom (2,1), while a queue enumerates front to back (2,3).

questions.prompt: Predict the output: mutating an object after adding it to a HashSet.
questions.explanation: The set placed k in the bucket for hash 1. After Id changes to 2, Contains(k) looks in the bucket for hash 2 and finds nothing: False, even though the object is still inside (Count is 1). Looking up Id = 1 finds the right bucket, but Equals compares against the mutated object (Id 2) and fails: False. Keys must not change while in a hashed collection.

questions.prompt: Predict the output: a static field in a generic class used with different type arguments.
questions.explanation: Each closed generic type (Counter<int>, Counter<string>, Counter<long>) is a separate type with its own copy of the static field. Counter<int> was incremented twice, Counter<string> once, and Counter<long> never.

questions.prompt: Predict the output: when a static constructor runs.
questions.explanation: A static constructor runs once, just before the type is first used. `start` prints first; the first access to Config.Value triggers the field initializer and then the static constructor body (`init`) and returns 42. The second access does not run it again.

questions.prompt: Predict the output: override versus `new` when called through a base-class reference.
questions.explanation: An override replaces the virtual slot, so calling Virt through a Base reference runs Derived.Virt. A `new` method only hides the base method: the compiler picks it by static type, so via `b` (typed Base) you get Base.Hide and via `d` (typed Derived) you get Derived.Hide.

questions.prompt: Predict the output: a virtual method called from a base-class constructor.
questions.explanation: Virtual dispatch works even inside the base constructor, so Derived.Show runs. In C#, field initializers of the derived class run before the base constructor is called, so `field` is already set, but the Derived constructor body has not run yet, so `set` is still null.

questions.prompt: Predict the output: an interface default method, with and without a class implementation.
questions.explanation: Plain does not implement Greet, so calling it through the interface uses the default body, which reads Plain's Name. Custom has a public Greet that implicitly implements the interface member, so it replaces the default.

questions.prompt: Predict the output: a class with an overloaded + operator, ==, and +=.
questions.explanation: The overloaded + returns a new Money with 12. Overloading + does not overload ==, so == on a class is reference equality: False. `c += b` means `c = c + b`, which points c at a new object; `a` is unchanged at 5, while c is 12.

questions.prompt: Predict the output: an extension method with the same name as an instance method, and one called on null.
questions.expectedOutput:
instance Say
extension Shout
extension on null
questions.explanation: Instance methods always win over extension methods with the same signature, so t.Say() runs the instance method. Shout exists only as an extension. Extension calls are just static calls with the receiver as the first argument, so calling one on null does not throw a NullReferenceException.

questions.prompt: Predict the output: nested using blocks and a using declaration.
questions.expectedOutput:
open A
open B
body
close B
close A
open C
end
close C
questions.explanation: Resources are disposed in reverse order of acquisition: B is closed before A, right after the block. A using declaration (`using var`) disposes at the end of the enclosing scope, here the end of the top-level statements, so `close C` comes after `end`.

questions.prompt: Predict the output: calling a mutating method on a struct stored in a readonly field.
questions.explanation: To protect a readonly struct field, the compiler calls methods on a defensive copy, so frozen.Inc() increments a temporary and the field stays 0. The non-readonly field is called in place and reaches 2. This hidden copy is also a performance cost; marking the struct `readonly` avoids it.

questions.prompt: Predict the output: passing an int and an array by value versus by ref.
questions.explanation: Inc receives a copy of a, so a stays 1; IncRef aliases b, so b becomes 2. An array reference is also passed by value: Reassign only changes its local copy of the reference, but Mutate writes through the reference into the shared array, so arr[0] is 7.

questions.prompt: Predict the output: ref locals and a method returning by ref.
questions.explanation: A ref local is an alias for a storage location, so assigning r writes arr[1] = 50. Largest returns a reference to the biggest element (50 at index 1), and assigning through that ref local sets it to 0, giving 1,0,3.
